title: Unlucky Strike: The Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid Was an Exceedingly Rare Meteorite
summary:
Sixty-six million years ago, a 10-to-15-kilometer-wide object slammed into Earth at roughly 64,000 km/h, ending the reign of the dinosaurs and wiping out 75 percent of all species. Now, an international team of scientists has identified the impactor as a rare type of meteorite known as a CO chondrite—a finding that reshapes our understanding of the catastrophe.

CO chondrites, or carbonaceous chondrites of the Ornans class, are among the most primitive materials in the solar system. They contain significantly fewer volatile elements like carbon, zinc, water, and especially sulfur compared to other meteorite classes. This detail is crucial: previous theories suggested that sulfur from the impactor vaporized and formed sunlight-blocking aerosols, causing a global winter. But the new study, published in Science Advances, indicates the impactor itself contributed relatively little sulfur. Instead, the primary driver of the mass extinction was likely the immense volume of fine debris ejected into the atmosphere.

Researchers from the University of British Columbia, Paris, Brussels, and Vienna reached this conclusion by measuring nickel isotopes in samples from the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary clay layer, which was deposited worldwide after the impact. 'Only a minute fraction of the projectile is preserved in the planet's KT clay layer because the entire meteorite vaporized upon impact,' explained Dr. Philippe Claeys, a visiting professor at UBC. The nickel isotope signature provided a precise chemical fingerprint, narrowing the impactor's identity to a CO chondrite—a class that accounts for only a small portion of the already rare carbonaceous chondrites, which make up just five percent of meteorites found on Earth.

The meteorite's origin remains uncertain; it may have come from the outer asteroid belt near Jupiter or even farther out in the solar system. 'Being impacted by such a rare, distant projectile really underscores how unlucky the dinosaurs were,' Claeys added. The impact created the Chicxulub crater, now buried beneath Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. This discovery not only refines the extinction narrative but also highlights the value of isotopic analysis in decoding Earth's violent past.
why_it_matters: This discovery matters because it changes the story of the most famous extinction event: it wasn't just any asteroid but an extraordinarily rare one, suggesting that mass extinctions can be linked to how unusual an impactor is. Understanding the exact cause helps us model past climate catastrophes and better appreciate Earth's vulnerability to space objects.

keywords.explanation: A very rare type of ancient space rock from the early solar system, low in sulfur and carbon.
Chemical building blocks that easily turn into gas, like water or carbon, which can affect climate when heated.
Tiny solid or liquid particles floating in the air, like mist or smoke, that can block sunlight when they spread high in the atmosphere.
Different forms of nickel atoms that have slightly different weights; measuring them helps identify what kind of meteorite hit Earth.
A thin layer of rock in the ground all over the world that marks the exact time when the dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago.
The giant, hidden circular scar on the Yucatán Peninsula where the asteroid struck, now buried under newer rock layers.

background_read: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs struck at a time when Earth was already stressed by massive volcanic eruptions in India (the Deccan Traps), which some scientists think also contributed to the extinction.
The Chicxulub crater (named after a Mexican town near the impact site, on the Yucatán Peninsula) is about 150 km wide and was discovered in the 1970s by geologists looking for oil.
Carbonaceous chondrites, especially the rare CO type, contain materials virtually unchanged since the birth of the solar system 4.6 billion years ago, making them valuable time capsules.
The study used nickel isotopes because the impactor was vaporized on contact, leaving almost no solid fragments—only a fine layer of dust containing its chemical signature settled globally.

Dr. Philippe Claeys, a planetary geologist at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Belgium) and a visiting professor at the University of British Columbia (UBC), specializes in impact events and mass extinctions.

perspectives.description: The finding settles a long-standing debate about whether sulfur or debris caused the dinosaur-killing climate collapse. It opens the door to using isotope fingerprints to identify ancient impactors, deepening our knowledge of Earth's history.

Some scientists caution that even tiny amounts of sulfur from the vaporized asteroid could still have had important effects. Focusing only on ejected debris might oversimplify complex, cascading environmental changes.

The study shows how an interdisciplinary mix of geology, chemistry, and astronomy is needed to solve deep-time mysteries. The extreme rarity of CO chondrites highlights the role of chance in cosmic events and the fragility of life.

Future missions to sample asteroid material, along with finer analysis of the K-Pg boundary layer, could reveal more about the impact's fallout. This knowledge might eventually help us prepare for—or even deflect—a future asteroid threat.
